response:
The central question is whether the geometric structure of the learned embedding space — specifically how "curved" it is and how much shortest paths (geodesics) deviate from straight Euclidean lines — predicts how well a contrastive model like CLIP generalizes to inputs outside its training distribution. In contrastive pretraining, image and text encoders are trained to align paired representations while pushing unpaired ones apart; the resulting manifold is not flat, and the curvature varies considerably across regions, often concentrating around the boundaries of semantic clusters. Key concepts are Riemannian curvature of the learned manifold (sectional and Ricci), the pullback metric induced by the encoder, geodesic deviation (Jacobi fields measuring how nearby geodesics spread or focus), and the distinction between in-distribution interpolation versus out-of-distribution extrapolation along those paths. A beginner assumes that a low contrastive loss means the space is well-behaved everywhere, but an expert worries that contrastive objectives are indifferent to geometry in low-density regions — the loss only constrains the space where training pairs land, leaving vast "dark" regions whose curvature is essentially arbitrary and ungoverned. The practical danger is that OOD inputs often map into precisely those dark regions, and a model that appears to generalize (because test accuracy is measured on another curated benchmark) may be traveling through geometrically distorted corridors where small input perturbations cause wildly disproportionate semantic jumps.

response:
The modality gap is not a structureless void — Liang et al. (2022) showed it is a cone-shaped region on the hypersphere with image embeddings and text embeddings occupying antipodal caps separated by roughly 0.8–1.2 units in cosine distance, and crucially the gap region has measurably lower embedding density and higher local curvature variation than either unimodal cluster, making it geometrically the most unreliable part of the joint space. You can measure the gap's curvature structure by computing sectional curvatures along geodesics that cross it — practically, by fitting a Riemannian metric to a 
𝑘
k-NN graph that includes both modalities and measuring how Jacobi fields evolve along cross-modal paths — and what you find is that the gap acts like a saddle region with negative sectional curvature, meaning nearby cross-modal geodesics diverge rather than converge, amplifying small perturbations into large semantic jumps. Fine-tuning interventions that close the gap, like CLIP-FT with contrastive loss on domain-specific paired data, do shift OOD generalization but not always in the expected direction: Wortsman et al. (2022) showed that naive fine-tuning on a target distribution collapses the gap locally while catastrophically increasing curvature in the rest of the joint space, degrading OOD performance on held-out domains by 5–15% even when in-distribution accuracy improves. The more surgical approach is WiSE-FT (Wortsman et al., 2022), which interpolates between pretrained and fine-tuned weights — this can be understood geometrically as partially reshaping the gap without fully collapsing it, preserving the low-curvature corridors that support cross-domain generalization. The predictable pattern that emerges is that the gap's width is less important than its curvature homogeneity: models where the cross-modal transition region has consistent, low sectional curvature generalize better OOD regardless of absolute gap size, suggesting that fine-tuning objectives should explicitly target curvature smoothness in the gap rather than just alignment of paired embeddings.
